chunks: First: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: Whichever man is killed by the fixed punishment (hadd) or by retribution (qisas), he has no blood money (diyah) due to him.

Second: Ali, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, from Mufaddal ibn Salih, from Zayd al-Shahham said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who was killed by retribution (qisas), does he have a blood money? He said: If that were the case, retribution would not be taken from anyone. And whoever is killed by the fixed punishment (hadd), he has no blood money. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: These two reports came in the same year, and it is appropriate that we specify them by saying: If he is killed by a fixed punishment of God, he has no blood money from the treasury (bayt al-mal), and if he dies from something of the human fixed punishments, his blood money is upon the treasury. This indicates it.

Third: What al-Hasan ibn Mahbub narrated from al-Hasan ibn Salih al-Thawri, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: Ali (peace be upon him) used to say: Whoever we strike with a fixed punishment of God and he dies, there is no blood money for us [to pay], and whoever we strike with a fixed punishment in something of the rights of people and he dies, then his blood money is upon us.

key_terms.دِيَة: Blood money paid to the victim's heirs

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on blood money if a person dies during the execution of Islamic corporal punishment?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Isfarayini clarifies the distinction between hudud of Allah (divine fixed punishments) and hudud of humans (judicial discretion), a key debate in Shia jurisprudence regarding state liability for death during punishment. Imam al-Sadiq (as) and Imam Ali (as) establish that while no blood money is owed for death from divine hudud, the treasury (bayt al-mal) bears the cost for human rights hudud, reflecting the principle of 'sahh al-dam' (validity of blood). This ruling ensures that the state assumes financial responsibility for errors or deaths in discretionary punishments, distinguishing them from the absolute nature of divine retribution.
